# Bellmer La Poupée: The Anatomical Anagram and the Surrealist Object
## I. Introduction: The Articulated Unconscious
The artistic oeuvre of Hans Bellmer (1902–1975) is dominated by a singular, obsession-fueled creation that has come to define the darker, more psychoanalytically rigorous currents of the Surrealist movement: *La Poupée* (The Doll). Conceived in the politically volatile atmosphere of Berlin in 1933 and subsequently refined in Paris, the Doll project is not a static sculpture but a dynamic, protean apparatus—a machine for the production of desire and the deconstruction of the human form Spanning photography, sculpture, drawing, and theoretical text, *La Poupée* represents one of the 20th century's most radical assaults on the integrity of the classical body, operating simultaneously as a mechanism of private erotic fixation and a public political statement against the "armored" aesthetic of German Fascism .

Bellmer's project, which evolved through two distinct physical iterations and numerous photographic series, posits the body not as a fixed biological destiny but as a linguistic structure—an "anagram" capable of infinite rearrangement By introducing the mechanical principle of the ball joint ( *jointure à boule* ) into the anatomy of a life-sized pubescent effigy, Bellmer sought to liberate somatic expression from the tyranny of anatomical necessity. In doing so, he created images that function, in his own terminology, as a "physical unconscious," where the centers of gravity within the body are displaced and reorganized according to the subjective intensities of pain, pleasure, and obsession .

The history of *La Poupée* is inextricably bound to the biography of its creator, the intellectual ferment of the interwar avant-garde, and the catastrophic rise of the Third Reich. From its genesis in a rejection of paternal authority and utilitarian labor to its embrace by the Parisian Surrealists André Breton and Paul Éluard, the Doll serves as a complex historical document. It is an object that embodies the "convulsive beauty" championed by the Surrealists—a beauty compounded of the erotic and the traumatic, the mechanical and the organic, the familiar and the uncanny This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the Doll's construction, its theoretical underpinnings, its publication history from *Die Puppe* (1934) to *Les Jeux de la poupée* (1949), and its enduring critical legacy.

## II. Biographical Matrix: The Engineer of Revolt
### 2.1 The Crisis of Paternal Authority
To understand the violent reconfiguration of the body in Bellmer's work, one must first examine the rigid structures he sought to dismantle. Hans Bellmer was born in Kattowitz, Silesia (then part of the German Empire), a region dominated by heavy industry and mining His relationship with his father was defined by a profound and antagonism that would become the psychoanalytic engine of his art. Bellmer's father was a severe, humorless figure, a symbol of bourgeois rectitude who would eventually join the Nazi Party—a trajectory that Bellmer viewed as the ultimate betrayal of human liberty .

This paternal conflict was not merely domestic; it was systemic. The father represents the Law, the State, and the "Reality Principle" that repressed desire and imagination. Bellmer's rebellion began early; Following arrests in his youth for "inciting workers to Socialist rebellion" and "undermining the moral support of the State," he was forced by his father to study engineering at the Berlin Technische Hochschule in 1923 While Bellmer would eventually abandon this path to work as a typographer and draftsman, the technical training he received was crucial. It provides him with the rigorous understanding of mechanics, perspective, and construction that will later allow him to build the intricate armatures of the Doll. The irony of Bellmer's career lies in this appropriation: he utilized the tools of the father (engineering, precision, calculation) to construct an object of pure irrationality and desire .

### 2.2 The Refusal of Utility
The catalyst for the Doll's creation was explicitly political. With the rise of Adolf Hitler and the National Socialist Party in 1933, Bellmer made a definitive vow: he will cease all work that could be "useful to the State" This refusal of utility was a radical artistic stance. In a society that was increasingly mobilizing every aspect of life—industry, bodies, art—for the service of the Reich, Bellmer withdrew into the private, the obsessive, and the useless. The construction of the Doll was an act of "inner emigration," a turning away from the monumental, healthy, productive bodies celebrated by Nazi propaganda (such as the sculptures of Arno Breker) toward a private world of disintegration, mutation, and erotic play .

### 2.3 The Tripartite Catalyst of 1932–1933
Scholarship on Bellmer identifies a convergence of three distinct events in the early 1930s that transformed his rebellion into a specific creative output. These events operate as a "primal scene" for the Doll's genesis, blending nostalgia, eroticism, and theatricality.

The Arrival of Ursula Naguschewski: 
In 1932, Bellmer's cousin, Ursula Naguschewski, arrived in Berlin from Kassel to stay with the family. Accounts of her age vary slightly, placing her between fifteen and seventeen years old—precisely on the threshold between the "pubescent" and the adult . Bellmer became infatuated with her. As a cousin, she represented a forbidden object of desire, a taboo that heightened the erotic charge of their interactions. Ursula was, by many accounts, a willing participant in the "game," described as flirting with Bellmer and exercising a "sexual fascination" over him . However, her unattainability (and perhaps the societal strictures against such a union) necessitated a displacement of desire. The Doll would become the surrogate for Ursula, a "cathartic surrogate" that allowed Bellmer to manipulate and possess the object of his affection in effigy . 
The Box of Childhood Toys: 
Around the same time, Bellmer received a shipment from his mother containing a crate of his childhood toys. This event triggered a flood of nostalgia, reconnecting the adult artist with the "magical thinking" of childhood . In the world of the child, the inanimate object is never truly dead; it possesses a latent life, a soul projected onto it by the child’s imagination. This rediscovery of the toy provided the material context for the Doll: it legitimized the use of "play" as a serious artistic strategy. The Doll would be, in essence, a toy for an adult, but one stripped of innocence and charged with the complexities of adult sexuality. 
The Tales of Hoffmann: 
The third and perhaps most aesthetically decisive catalyst was a performance of Jacques Offenbach’s opera The Tales of Hoffmann (based on the stories of E.T.A. Hoffmann), which Bellmer attended in 1932\. The production, directed by the legendary Max Reinhardt at the Grosses Schauspielhaus, featured the famous first act in which the protagonist falls in love with the automaton Olympia . The tragic climax of this act, in which Olympia is revealed to be a machine and is torn limb from limb, had a profound impact on Bellmer. He watched with a mixture of "fascination and horror" as the object of desire was dismembered . This scene provided the "visual and plastic possibilities" for the Doll project. It suggested that dismemberment was not the end of the object, but a condition of its existence—that the artificial woman could be taken apart and put back together, and that this fragmentability was central to her allure .

## III. The First Doll (1933–1934): The Interior Gaze
Driven by these converging forces, Bellmer began construction of the first Doll in 1933, enlisting the help of his brother Fritz, who, like Hans, was a trained engineer . This collaboration between brothers on a project of such intense erotic fixation adds another layer to the psychological complexity of the work, suggesting a shared retreat into the fantasies of childhood.

### 3.1 Materiality and Construction
The First Doll was a "wood-and-metal skeleton covered with a realistic body of plaster and papier mâché" . The choice of materials was significant: plaster and papier-mâché are rigid, brittle materials associated with traditional doll-making and theater props. They allowed for a high degree of naturalism in the modeling of the surface—Bellmer could sculpt the curves of the torso, the details of the hands, and the features of the face with precision.

The figure was life-sized, modeled directly on the proportions of a young girl (presumably Ursula). It was articulated, but its movement was limited compared to the later iteration. The articulation relied on a system of bolts and hinges that allowed the limbs to be posed, but the torso remained a relatively fixed container .

### 3.2 The Mechanism of the Panorama
The defining feature of the First Doll—and the one that most clearly links it to the theme of the "unconscious"—was a mechanism installed inside the torso. Bellmer designed the doll with a series of "panoramas" or miniature dioramas located in the stomach . These internal scenes were illuminated by small electric lights, which could be activated by pressing a button concealed in the doll’s nipple .

This mechanism is a literalization of the psychoanalytic concept of "interiority." It invites the viewer to look *inside* the object of desire, transforming the female body into a peep-show box. The act of pressing the nipple to see the "secrets" of the belly connects the tactile (the erotic touch) with the scopophilic (the drive to look). It suggests that the truth of the subject lies deep within the visceral cavity, illuminated only for the voyeur who knows how to trigger the mechanism.

However, Bellmer found this design technically flawed. The panoramas made the doll "too cumbersome" and heavy . The rigidity of the torso necessary to house the mechanism prevented the kind of radical reconfiguration he was beginning to envision. The "magic" of the interior scenes was too static; Bellmer sought a magic that was structural, a mutability that could be enacted on the body's very architecture.

### 3.3 The Photographic Record: *Die Puppe* (1934)
Bellmer documented the First Doll in a series of approximately 30 black-and-white photographs . These images do not merely record the finished object; they document the *process* of its assembly and disassembly. We see the wooden skeleton, the hollow shell of the torso, the detached limbs scattered like the aftermath of a violent event.

In 1934, Bellmer self-published ten of these photographs in a small book titled *Die Puppe* (The Doll) . The publication was a clandestine affair, printed in Karlsruhe with the assistance of his friend Thomas Eckstein .

* **Anonymity:** Given the political climate and the "degenerate" nature of the imagery, Bellmer published the work without a publisher's imprint, keeping the circulation extremely limited (estimates range from 10 to 50 copies) . 
* **Dedication:** The book bore a dedication "Für Ursula N." alongside the title page, explicitly acknowledging the muse who inspired the project . 
* **Format:** The photographs were "tipped-in" (pasted by hand) onto the pages, creating an album-like intimacy. The text, written by Bellmer, was titled "Erinnerungen zum Thema Puppe" (Memories of the Doll Theme) . This text is a feverish, poetic exploration of childhood memory, describing the "struggle with a trauma from his youth" and the obsessive affection for his cousin .

This small book was the first signal flare sent out from Bellmer’s isolation in Nazi Germany to the wider European avant-garde.

## IV. The Second Doll (1935): The Ball Joint and the Anagram
If the First Doll was about *interiority* (the panorama), the Second Doll was about *permutability*. In 1935, Bellmer abandoned the rigid torso of the first model and constructed a new figure based on a radically different mechanical principle .

### 4.1 The Revelation of the Ball Joint
The conceptual breakthrough for the Second Doll came from a visit to the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum in Berlin, where Bellmer encountered a pair of articulated dolls from the era of Albrecht Dürer (16th century) . These historical figures were constructed around a central spherical joint—a "ball joint" (*jointure à boule*)—that allowed for articulation in all directions.

Bellmer seized upon this mechanism as the solution to the limitations of the First Doll. He realized that a central ball joint could serve as a universal connector. It dismantled the hierarchy of the human body, where the vertical axis (spine) dictates the arrangement of limbs. With the ball joint, the body became a modular system.

### 4.2 The Anatomy of the Second Doll
The Second Doll was constructed not of plaster, but of a mixture of glue and tissue paper painted to resemble flesh . This material shift was crucial: the new surface was softer, more tactile, and more "lifelike" than the hard carapace of the first doll. It responded to light in a way that mimicked skin, enhancing the uncanny realism of the photographs.

The anatomy of this new figure was radically expanded:

* **The Central Joint:** A spherical belly that could connect to multiple pelvises or torsos . 
* **Multiplicity:** The doll possessed "an extra torso and a pair of arms and legs," as well as "four spherical breasts" . 
* **Reversibility:** The most disturbing aspect of the Second Doll was its reversibility. A pelvis could be attached to another pelvis; a pair of legs could replace the head. Bellmer constructed "cephalopods"—monsters consisting of a head attached directly to a pair of legs, or a headless torso with legs radiating from both ends .

### 4.3 The Theory of the Anagram
Bellmer articulated the theoretical implications of this construction through the metaphor of the *anagram*. In language, an anagram is the rearrangement of the letters of a word to form a new word (e.g., the name *Unica* rearranged). Bellmer argued that the body is "like an endless sentence that invites us to rearrange it" .

By treating the limbs, breasts, and organs as "letters" in a somatic alphabet, Bellmer could spell out new meanings. A leg is not just a leg; in a different position, it might become a phallus, an arm, or a breast. This "anatomical anagram" suggests that identity is not fixed by nature but is a fluid construction of desire. "The body," Bellmer wrote, "is comparable to a sentence that invites you to disarticulate it, so that its true contents may be recomposed through an endless series of anagrams" . This concept of the anagram would become central to his later collaboration with the poet and artist Unica Zürn, who produced extensive anagrammatic poetry .

## V. Photographic Tableaux: The Aesthetic of the Crime Scene
While the Dolls existed as physical objects, their primary mode of existence was photographic. Bellmer did not exhibit the dolls as sculptures in the 1930s; rather, he staged them in elaborate tableaux which were then photographed. This mediation was essential. Photography allowed Bellmer to control the gaze absolutely, to frame the object, to manipulate the lighting, and to impose a specific narrative context.

### 5.1 The Domestic Uncanny
A significant portion of the Doll photographs are set in domestic interiors: the kitchen, the bedroom, the stairwell, the attic . These settings are crucial for generating the *Unheimliche* (the uncanny). Freud defined the uncanny as something familiar (*heimlich*) that has become strange or repressed. By placing the mutilated, hyper-sexualized doll in the banal setting of a German home—next to a carpet beater, a bed frame, or a window—Bellmer suggests that the horror is not external, but internal to the domestic sphere . The "innocent" violence of the nursery and the repressed sexuality of the family structure are dragged into the light.

### 5.2 The Forest and Surveillance (1936)
In a notable series from 1936, Bellmer moved the Doll outdoors, into a forest setting. One hand-colored photograph from this series depicts a headless torso with four legs (two sets of black leather shoes) standing among the trees. Lurking behind a tree in the background is "an ominous and voyeuristic figure dressed in all black," presumably Bellmer himself .

This image has been interpreted as a commentary on the "suffocating environment of surveillance" in Nazi Germany. The Doll is exposed, vulnerable, a specimen in the wild, while the dark figure watches. It evokes the predation of the state upon the individual, but also the artist’s own predatory gaze upon his creation .

### 5.3 Chromatic Intervention: The Hand-Colored Prints
Bellmer frequently hand-colored his gelatin silver prints using aniline dyes or "candy-colored pastels" . This practice was unusual for art photography of the time, which largely adhered to the modernist "truth" of black and white. The addition of color—pinks, yellows, purples—gave the images a heightened, artificial quality.

This coloring was not merely decorative. It often gave the Doll’s skin a "diseased" or bruised appearance . At a time when Nazi ideology was obsessed with the "healthy" Aryan body, the clean skin, and the purity of blood, Bellmer’s coloring emphasized the artificial, the cosmetic, and the pathological. It was a "protest against the desire for perfection in Nazi 'body culture'" . The colors were often "acidic" or "garish," disrupting the realism of the photograph and pushing it toward the realm of the hallucination.

## VI. Publication and Dissemination: From Berlin to Paris
The migration of the Doll from a private obsession in Berlin to a public scandal in Paris occurred through a specific network of Surrealist publications.

### 6.1 *Minotaure* (1934)
The bridge between Bellmer and the Surrealists was Ursula Naguschewski. In 1934, she traveled to Paris, where she was a student at the Sorbonne, and brought the photographs of the First Doll to André Breton, the "Pope" of Surrealism . Breton was immediately captivated. The images seemed to perfectly embody the Surrealist concept of the "fetish" and the "marvelous."

In December 1934, the prestigious Surrealist journal *Minotaure* published a two-page spread of 18 photographs of the Doll . The title of the feature was "Poupée: Variations sur le montage d'une mineure articulée" (Doll: Variations on the Assemblage of an Articulated Minor) . This publication was a watershed moment. It placed Bellmer instantly at the center of the movement, alongside figures like Dali, Man Ray, and Max Ernst. The "articulated minor" became a new icon of the movement, representing the subversion of the rational adult world.

### 6.2 *La Poupée* (Editions G.L.M., 1936\)
Following the success in *Minotaure*, a dedicated French edition of Bellmer’s book was published in Paris in 1936\.

* **Publisher:** Editions G.L.M. (Guy Lévis-Mano), a key publisher of Surrealist texts . 
* **Translation:** The German text "Erinnerungen zum Thema Puppe" was translated into French by Robert Valençay . 
* **Format:** The edition was limited to approximately 100 copies (some sources state 105). A distinctive feature of this edition was the use of pink paper for the text pages, enhancing the "fleshly" and feminine association of the book . 
* **Content:** It contained ten original gelatin silver prints tipped in, maintaining the album format of the German original .

### 6.3 *Les Jeux de la poupée* (1949)
The most comprehensive publication of the Doll photographs was conceived in the late 1930s but delayed by the outbreak of World War II. It was finally published in 1949 as *Les Jeux de la poupée* (The Games of the Doll) .

* **Collaboration:** This volume was a collaboration between Bellmer and the poet Paul Éluard. Éluard selected 14 photographs of the Second Doll and wrote 14 prose poems (*quatorze poèmes*) to accompany them . 
* **Hand-Coloring:** The edition (limited to 136 copies) featured original photographs that were hand-colored not just by Bellmer, but with the assistance of friends including the artist Christian d'Orgeix and reportedly Éluard himself . 
* **Preface:** The book included a dense theoretical introduction by Bellmer titled "Notes on the Subject of the Ball Joint" (*Notes au sujet de la jointure à boule*), written in 1938 and translated/adapted with Georges Hugnet . This text provides the "pseudo-scientific" rationale for the Doll’s anatomy, discussing the "physics of passion" and the geometry of the joint.

## VII. Political Dimensions: The Body Anti-Fascist
The political content of *La Poupée* is often overshadowed by its eroticism, but for Bellmer, the two were inseparable. The Doll was a "machine-gunneress in a state of grace" (a title of a 1937 work), a weapon aimed at the ideological foundations of the Third Reich .

### 7.1 Hal Foster and the Armored Body
The art historian Hal Foster has provided one of the most influential readings of Bellmer’s politics. In his analysis of "Armored Bodies," Foster contrasts the Surrealist body with the Fascist body. The Nazi aesthetic, exemplified by the official state art, fetishized the "armored" body: the male body as a seamless, rigid, impenetrable statue . This body represented the solidity of the State, the purity of the Race, and the invulnerability of the Leader.

Bellmer’s Doll is the anti-armor. It is soft, fragmented, permeable, and constantly falling apart. It celebrates "degeneracy"—the very quality the Nazis sought to purge. By presenting the body as a site of trauma, mutation, and fluid identity, Bellmer actively sabotaged the fascist ideal of wholeness . The Doll is "indigestible" to fascism because it cannot be disciplined; its very structure is one of disobedience.

### 7.2 The Degenerate Art Context
In 1937, the Nazis staged the infamous "Degenerate Art" (*Entartete Kunst*) exhibition, mocking modern art. While Bellmer was not the primary target of this specific show (being less famous in Germany than the Expressionists), his work was spiritual kin to the "degeneracy" on display. The Nazis viewed modernism as a symptom of racial and mental decay. Bellmer embraced this "decay" as a form of resistance. If the Nazis demanded a "healthy" body, Bellmer would give them a "diseased" one. If they demanded a "productive" body, he would give them a useless one, devoted only to the non-productive expenditure of eroticism .

## VIII. The Paris Years and Exile (1938–1975)
In 1938, a personal tragedy precipitated Bellmer’s final departure from Germany. His wife Margarete, who had been a conspirator in the Doll project (even helping to build the first one), died of tuberculosis . With her death, the last tie to Berlin was severed. Bellmer moved to Paris, taking the Doll (or parts of it) with him in a suitcase .

### 8.1 The International Surrealist Exhibition (1938)
Upon arriving in Paris, Bellmer was immediately integrated into the planning for the *Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme* (International Surrealist Exhibition) of 1938, held at the Galerie Beaux-Arts . This exhibition is legendary in art history for its immersive design by Marcel Duchamp (who hung coal sacks from the ceiling) and the "Street of Mannequins" in the hallway.

Bellmer was one of the artists invited to dress a mannequin for this street. While many artists (like Masson and Dali) decorated their mannequins with found objects, Bellmer’s contribution was deeply consistent with his own practice, treating the mannequin as a site of violation and reconstruction . The exhibition solidified his status as the "master of the mannequin" within the group.

### 8.2 Internment and the War
The outbreak of World War II in 1939 turned Bellmer from a celebrated guest into an "enemy alien." Despite his anti-Nazi stance, he was a German citizen. In 1939, he was arrested by the French authorities and interned at the Camp des Milles near Aix-en-Provence, a brick factory converted into a prison camp .

At Les Milles, Bellmer was interned alongside other German artists, including Max Ernst and Wols. The conditions were difficult, but artistic production continued. Bellmer drew, often using the brick architecture of the camp as a motif in his "anamorphic" portraits. He was eventually released but lived in precarious conditions in the south of France before returning to Paris after the war .

### 8.3 Post-War: Bataille and Zurn
After the war, Bellmer abandoned the construction of new Dolls, though he continued to photograph and draw them. He shifted his focus to engraving and drawing, producing some of his most explicit work.

* **Georges Bataille:** In 1947, Bellmer collaborated with Georges Bataille on a new edition of *Story of the Eye*. The themes of the book—the equivalencies between the eye, the egg, and the testicle—resonated perfectly with Bellmer’s anagrammatic logic . 
* **Unica Zurn:** In 1953, Bellmer met Unica Zurn, a German writer and artist. She became his partner and model. Zurn’s practice of writing "anagram poems" paralleled Bellmer’s visual anagrams. Bellmer photographed Zurn bound with string, creating the "Unica" series, which transformed the living flesh into sections resembling the articulated segments of the Doll . Their relationship was intense and tragic, ending with Zurn’s suicide in 1970 and Bellmer’s decline until his death in 1975 .

## IX. Theoretical Anatomy: The Physical Unconscious
Bellmer’s work is not merely visual; it is a form of "corporeal philosophy." His major theoretical text, *Little Anatomy of the Physical Unconscious, or The Anatomy of the Image* (published in French in 1957), outlines the complex mechanics of his vision .

### 9.1 The Reflex and the Virtual Center
Bellmer argues that the body is governed by the "reflex." When a specific part of the body experiences intense sensation (pain, sexual arousal), the body’s "center of gravity" shifts to that point. If one has a toothache, the "ego" migrates to the tooth. Bellmer calls this the creation of a "virtual center" .

The Doll is an attempt to represent this invisible shifting of centers. If the desire is focused on the leg, the leg becomes the whole body. The "cephalopod" (head-leg creature) is a representation of a body where the brain (thought) is directly connected to the limb (action/flight/sex), bypassing the torso (digestion/heart).

### 9.2 The Image \= Magic
Bellmer was fascinated by the linguistic coincidence that the French word *IMAGE* is an anagram of *MAGIE* (Magic). He received a telegram from Man Ray pointing this out . For Bellmer, the image was indeed a form of magic—a way of casting a spell on reality to make it conform to desire. The Doll was a magical object, a totem used to ward off the reality of the father and the state, and to summon the "marvelous" into existence .

## X. Legacy: From Surrealism to the Post-Human
The legacy of *La Poupée* extends far beyond its Surrealist origins. It is a foundational text for the "Post-Human" in art.

### 10.1 Contemporary Resonances
* **Cindy Sherman:** Sherman’s "Sex Pictures" (1992) and mannequin works clearly dialogue with Bellmer. Like Bellmer, she uses medical prosthetics and doll parts to construct grotesque, sexualized bodies that interrogate the "male gaze" while simultaneously inhabiting it . 
* **The Chapman Brothers:** Jake and Dinos Chapman’s *Zygotic Acceleration* (1995) features child mannequins fused together, with genitalia displaced to their faces. This is a direct sculptural application of Bellmer’s anagrammatic theory—the displacement of the erogenous zone to create a "monstrous" new organism . 
* **Anime and Cyberpunk:** The image of the articulated, artificial girl has permeated pop culture, notably in Mamoru Oshii’s *Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence* (2004), which features dolls that are visual descendants of Bellmer’s creations .

### 10.2 Feminist Critique
Feminist reception of Bellmer has been divided. Early critiques often viewed the Doll as a supreme example of misogyny—the literal objectification and dismemberment of the female body for male pleasure . The violence of the images is undeniable. However, scholars like Sue Taylor and Therese Lichtenstein have argued for a more complex reading. They suggest that Bellmer *identifies* with the Doll. The Doll is not "other"; it is a self-portrait. Through the Doll, Bellmer explores his own passivity, his own castration anxiety, and his own desire to be "unmade" and "remade" . The Doll allows for a fluidity of gender where the male artist can inhabit the female form to escape the rigid expectations of masculinity (the "armored body") imposed by his father and the state.

## XI. Conclusion: The Endless Sentence
Hans Bellmer’s *La Poupée* remains one of the most disturbing and intellectually rigorous projects of the 20th century. It is a work that refuses to resolve itself. It is at once a toy and a weapon, a love letter and a crime scene, a photograph and a sculpture.

By applying the engineer’s precision to the chaotic materials of the unconscious, Bellmer created a "mechanics of desire" that exposed the fragility of human identity. The Doll demonstrates that the body is not a fixed fact, but a sentence waiting to be written—an anagram that can be scrambled to reveal the hidden demons and delights of the psyche. In the shadow of the Holocaust and the total war of the 1930s and 40s, Bellmer’s dismantled mannequins stand as a silent, terrifying witness to the disintegration of the humanist subject, offering in its place a beauty that is, as Breton demanded, truly convulsive.

| **Date of Construction** | 1933–1934 | 1935 |

La Poupée has come to define the darker, more psychoanalytically rigorous currents of the Surrealist movement.

The Doll project is not a static sculpture but a dynamic, protean apparatus—a machine for the production of desire and the deconstruction of the human form.
*La Poupée* spans photography, sculpture, drawing, and theoretical text.

*La Poupée* operates simultaneously as a mechanism of private erotic fixation and a public political statement against the "armored" aesthetic of German Fascism.

From its genesis in a rejection of paternal authority and utilitarian labor to its embrace by the Parisian Surrealists André Breton and Paul Éluard, the Doll serves as a complex historical document.

The Doll is an object that embodies the "convulsive beauty" championed by the Surrealists—a beauty compounded of the erotic and the traumatic, the mechanical and the organic, the familiar and the uncanny.

This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the Doll's construction, its theoretical underpinnings, its publication history from *Die Puppe* (1934) to *Les Jeux de la poupée* (1949), and its enduring critical legacy.
Hans Bellmer was born in Kattowitz, Silesia (then part of the German Empire), a region dominated by heavy industry and mining.
Bellmer's relationship with his father was defined by a profound antagonism that would become the psychoanalytic engine of his art.
Bellmer's father was a severe, humorless figure, a symbol of bourgeois rectitude who would eventually join the Nazi Party.
Bellmer viewed his father's trajectory of joining the Nazi Party as the ultimate betrayal of human liberty.
Bellmer's rebellion began early.

Bellmer was forced by his father to study engineering at the Berlin Technische Hochschule in 1923, following arrests in his youth for "inciting workers to Socialist rebellion" and "undermining the moral support of the State."
Bellmer would eventually abandon his engineering path to work as a typographer and draftsman.

The technical training Bellmer received was crucial, providing him with a rigorous understanding of mechanics, perspective, and construction that would later allow him to build the intricate armatures of the Doll.
The irony of Bellmer's career lies in his appropriation of the tools of the father (engineering, precision, calculation) to construct an object of pure irrationality and desire.
The catalyst for the Doll's creation was explicitly political.
With the rise of Adolf Hitler and the National Socialist Party in 1933, Bellmer made a definitive vow to cease all work that could be "useful to the State."
Bellmer's refusal of utility was a radical artistic stance.
In a society that was increasingly mobilizing every aspect of life—industry, bodies, art—for the service of the Reich, Bellmer withdrew into the private, the obsessive, and the useless.

The construction of the Doll was an act of "inner emigration," a turning away from the monumental, healthy, productive bodies celebrated by Nazi propaganda (such as the sculptures of Arno Breker) toward a private world of disintegration, mutation, and erotic play.
Scholarship on Bellmer identifies a convergence of three distinct events in the early 1930s that transformed his rebellion into a specific creative output.
These events operate as a "primal scene" for the Doll's genesis, blending nostalgia, eroticism, and theatricality.
In 1932, Bellmer's cousin, Ursula Naguschewski, arrived in Berlin from Kassel to stay with the family.
Accounts of Ursula Naguschewski's age vary slightly, placing her between fifteen and seventeen years old—precisely on the threshold between the "pubescent" and the adult.
Bellmer became infatuated with Ursula Naguschewski.
As a cousin, Ursula Naguschewski represented a forbidden object of desire, a taboo that heightened the erotic charge of their interactions.
Ursula Naguschewski was, by many accounts, a willing participant in the "game," described as flirting with Bellmer and exercising a "sexual fascination" over him.
Ursula Naguschewski's unattainability (and perhaps the societal strictures against such a union) necessitated a displacement of desire.
The Doll would become the surrogate for Ursula Naguschewski, a "cathartic surrogate" that allowed Bellmer to manipulate and possess the object of his affection in effigy.
Around the same time, Bellmer received a shipment from his mother containing a crate of his childhood toys.
This event triggered a flood of nostalgia, reconnecting the adult artist with the "magical thinking" of childhood.
In the world of the child, the inanimate object is never truly dead; it possesses a latent life, a soul projected onto it by the child’s imagination.
This rediscovery of the toy provided the material context for the Doll: it legitimized the use of "play" as a serious artistic strategy.
The Doll would be, in essence, a toy for an adult, but one stripped of innocence and charged with the complexities of adult sexuality.

The third and perhaps most aesthetically decisive catalyst was a performance of Jacques Offenbach’s opera The Tales of Hoffmann (based on the stories of E.T.A. Hoffmann), which Bellmer attended in 1932.

The production of The Tales of Hoffmann, directed by the legendary Max Reinhardt at the Grosses Schauspielhaus, featured the famous first act in which the protagonist falls in love with the automaton Olympia.
The tragic climax of this act, in which Olympia is revealed to be a machine and is torn limb from limb, had a profound impact on Bellmer.
Bellmer watched the scene with a mixture of "fascination and horror" as the object of desire was dismembered.
This scene provided the "visual and plastic possibilities" for the Doll project.
The scene suggested that dismemberment was not the end of the object, but a condition of its existence.
The scene suggested that the artificial woman could be taken apart and put back together, and that this fragmentability was central to her allure.
Driven by these converging forces, Bellmer began construction of the first Doll in 1933.
Bellmer enlisted the help of his brother Fritz, who, like Hans, was a trained engineer, for the construction of the first Doll.

This collaboration between brothers on a project of such intense erotic fixation adds another layer to the psychological complexity of the work, suggesting a shared retreat into the fantasies of childhood.
The First Doll was a "wood-and-metal skeleton covered with a realistic body of plaster and papier mâché."
The choice of materials for the First Doll was significant.
Plaster and papier-mâché are rigid, brittle materials associated with traditional doll-making and theater props.

These materials allowed for a high degree of naturalism in the modeling of the surface, enabling Bellmer to sculpt the curves of the torso, the details of the hands, and the features of the face with precision.
The figure of the First Doll was life-sized, modeled directly on the proportions of a young girl (presumably Ursula).
The First Doll was articulated, but its movement was limited compared to the later iteration.
The articulation of the First Doll relied on a system of bolts and hinges that allowed the limbs to be posed, but the torso remained a relatively fixed container.
The defining feature of the First Doll was a mechanism installed inside the torso.
Bellmer designed the First Doll with a series of "panoramas" or miniature dioramas located in the stomach.
These internal scenes were illuminated by small electric lights, which could be activated by pressing a button concealed in the doll’s nipple.
This mechanism is a literalization of the psychoanalytic concept of "interiority."
It invites the viewer to look *inside* the object of desire, transforming the female body into a peep-show box.
The act of pressing the nipple to see the "secrets" of the belly connects the tactile (the erotic touch) with the scopophilic (the drive to look).
It suggests that the truth of the subject lies deep within the visceral cavity, illuminated only for the voyeur who knows how to trigger the mechanism.
Bellmer found this design technically flawed.
The panoramas made the doll "too cumbersome" and heavy.
The rigidity of the torso necessary to house the mechanism prevented the kind of radical reconfiguration Bellmer was beginning to envision.
The "magic" of the interior scenes was too static; Bellmer sought a magic that was structural, a mutability that could be enacted on the body's very architecture.
Bellmer documented the First Doll in a series of approximately 30 black-and-white photographs.
These images do not merely record the finished object; they document the *process* of its assembly and disassembly.
We see the wooden skeleton, the hollow shell of the torso, the detached limbs scattered like the aftermath of a violent event in these images.
In 1934, Bellmer self-published ten of these photographs in a small book titled *Die Puppe* (The Doll).
The publication of *Die Puppe* was a clandestine affair, printed in Karlsruhe with the assistance of his friend Thomas Eckstein.

Given the political climate and the "degenerate" nature of the imagery, Bellmer published *Die Puppe* without a publisher's imprint, keeping the circulation extremely limited (estimates range from 10 to 50 copies).
The book *Die Puppe* bore a dedication "Für Ursula N." alongside the title page, explicitly acknowledging the muse who inspired the project.
The photographs in *Die Puppe* were "tipped-in" (pasted by hand) onto the pages, creating an album-like intimacy.
The text in *Die Puppe*, written by Bellmer, was titled "Erinnerungen zum Thema Puppe" (Memories of the Doll Theme).
This text is a feverish, poetic exploration of childhood memory, describing the "struggle with a trauma from his youth" and the obsessive affection for his cousin.
This small book was the first signal flare sent out from Bellmer’s isolation in Nazi Germany to the wider European avant-garde.
If the First Doll was about *interiority* (the panorama), the Second Doll was about *permutability*.
In 1935, Bellmer abandoned the rigid torso of the first model and constructed a new figure based on a radically different mechanical principle.
The conceptual breakthrough for the Second Doll came from a visit to the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum in Berlin.
At the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, Bellmer encountered a pair of articulated dolls from the era of Albrecht Dürer (16th century).
These historical figures were constructed around a central spherical joint—a "ball joint" (*jointure à boule*)—that allowed for articulation in all directions.
Bellmer seized upon this mechanism as the solution to the limitations of the First Doll.
Bellmer realized that a central ball joint could serve as a universal connector.
The ball joint dismantled the hierarchy of the human body, where the vertical axis (spine) dictates the arrangement of limbs.
With the ball joint, the body became a modular system.
The Second Doll was constructed not of plaster, but of a mixture of glue and tissue paper painted to resemble flesh.
This material shift was crucial for the Second Doll.
The new surface of the Second Doll was softer, more tactile, and more "lifelike" than the hard carapace of the first doll.
The new surface responded to light in a way that mimicked skin, enhancing the uncanny realism of the photographs.
The anatomy of this new figure was radically expanded.
The Second Doll featured a spherical belly that could connect to multiple pelvises or torsos.
The Second Doll possessed "an extra torso and a pair of arms and legs," as well as "four spherical breasts."
The most disturbing aspect of the Second Doll was its reversibility.
A pelvis could be attached to another pelvis in the Second Doll.
A pair of legs could replace the head in the Second Doll.
Bellmer constructed "cephalopods"—monsters consisting of a head attached directly to a pair of legs, or a headless torso with legs radiating from both ends.
Bellmer articulated the theoretical implications of this construction through the metaphor of the *anagram*.
In language, an anagram is the rearrangement of the letters of a word to form a new word (e.g., the name *Unica* rearranged).
Bellmer argued that the body is "like an endless sentence that invites us to rearrange it."
By treating the limbs, breasts, and organs as "letters" in a somatic alphabet, Bellmer could spell out new meanings.
A leg is not just a leg; in a different position, it might become a phallus, an arm, or a breast.
This "anatomical anagram" suggests that identity is not fixed by nature but is a fluid construction of desire.
Bellmer wrote, "The body is comparable to a sentence that invites you to disarticulate it, so that its true contents may be recomposed through an endless series of anagrams."
This concept of the anagram would become central to Bellmer's later collaboration with the poet and artist Unica Zürn, who produced extensive anagrammatic poetry.
While the Dolls existed as physical objects, their primary mode of existence was photographic.
Bellmer did not exhibit the dolls as sculptures in the 1930s; rather, he staged them in elaborate tableaux which were then photographed.
This mediation was essential.
Photography allowed Bellmer to control the gaze absolutely, to frame the object, to manipulate the lighting, and to impose a specific narrative context.
A significant portion of the Doll photographs are set in domestic interiors: the kitchen, the bedroom, the stairwell, the attic.
These settings are crucial for generating the *Unheimliche* (the uncanny).
Freud defined the uncanny as something familiar (*heimlich*) that has become strange or repressed.

By placing the mutilated, hyper-sexualized doll in the banal setting of a German home—next to a carpet beater, a bed frame, or a window—Bellmer suggests that the horror is not external, but internal to the domestic sphere.
The "innocent" violence of the nursery and the repressed sexuality of the family structure are dragged into the light.
In a notable series from 1936, Bellmer moved the Doll outdoors, into a forest setting.
One hand-colored photograph from this series depicts a headless torso with four legs (two sets of black leather shoes) standing among the trees.
Lurking behind a tree in the background of this photograph is "an ominous and voyeuristic figure dressed in all black," presumably Bellmer himself.
This image has been interpreted as a commentary on the "suffocating environment of surveillance" in Nazi Germany.
The Doll is exposed, vulnerable, a specimen in the wild, while the dark figure watches.
It evokes the predation of the state upon the individual, but also the artist’s own predatory gaze upon his creation.
Bellmer frequently hand-colored his gelatin silver prints using aniline dyes or "candy-colored pastels."
This practice was unusual for art photography of the time, which largely adhered to the modernist "truth" of black and white.
The addition of color—pinks, yellows, purples—gave the images a heightened, artificial quality.
This coloring was not merely decorative.
The coloring often gave the Doll’s skin a "diseased" or bruised appearance.
At a time when Nazi ideology was obsessed with the "healthy" Aryan body, the clean skin, and the purity of blood, Bellmer’s coloring emphasized the artificial, the cosmetic, and the pathological.
It was a "protest against the desire for perfection in Nazi 'body culture'."
The colors were often "acidic" or "garish," disrupting the realism of the photograph and pushing it toward the realm of the hallucination.
The migration of the Doll from a private obsession in Berlin to a public scandal in Paris occurred through a specific network of Surrealist publications.
The bridge between Bellmer and the Surrealists was Ursula Naguschewski.
In 1934, Ursula Naguschewski traveled to Paris, where she was a student at the Sorbonne, and brought the photographs of the First Doll to André Breton, the "Pope" of Surrealism.
Breton was immediately captivated by the images.
The images seemed to perfectly embody the Surrealist concept of the "fetish" and the "marvelous."
In December 1934, the prestigious Surrealist journal *Minotaure* published a two-page spread of 18 photographs of the Doll.
The title of the feature was "Poupée: Variations sur le montage d'une mineure articulée" (Doll: Variations on the Assemblage of an Articulated Minor).
This publication was a watershed moment.
It placed Bellmer instantly at the center of the movement, alongside figures like Dali, Man Ray, and Max Ernst.
The "articulated minor" became a new icon of the movement, representing the subversion of the rational adult world.
Following the success in *Minotaure*, a dedicated French edition of Bellmer’s book was published in Paris in 1936.
The publisher of *La Poupée* (1936) was Editions G.L.M. (Guy Lévis-Mano), a key publisher of Surrealist texts.
The German text "Erinnerungen zum Thema Puppe" was translated into French by Robert Valençay for *La Poupée* (1936).
The edition of *La Poupée* (1936) was limited to approximately 100 copies (some sources state 105).
A distinctive feature of this edition was the use of pink paper for the text pages, enhancing the "fleshly" and feminine association of the book.
It contained ten original gelatin silver prints tipped in, maintaining the album format of the German original.
The most comprehensive publication of the Doll photographs was conceived in the late 1930s but delayed by the outbreak of World War II.
It was finally published in 1949 as *Les Jeux de la poupée* (The Games of the Doll).
*Les Jeux de la poupée* was a collaboration between Bellmer and the poet Paul Éluard.
Éluard selected 14 photographs of the Second Doll and wrote 14 prose poems (*quatorze poèmes*) to accompany them.

The edition of *Les Jeux de la poupée* (limited to 136 copies) featured original photographs that were hand-colored not just by Bellmer, but with the assistance of friends including the artist Christian d'Orgeix and reportedly Éluard himself.

The book included a dense theoretical introduction by Bellmer titled "Notes on the Subject of the Ball Joint" (*Notes au sujet de la jointure à boule*), written in 1938 and translated/adapted with Georges Hugnet.
This text provides the "pseudo-scientific" rationale for the Doll’s anatomy, discussing the "physics of passion" and the geometry of the joint.
The political content of *La Poupée* is often overshadowed by its eroticism, but for Bellmer, the two were inseparable.
The Doll was a "machine-gunneress in a state of grace" (a title of a 1937 work), a weapon aimed at the ideological foundations of the Third Reich.
The art historian Hal Foster has provided one of the most influential readings of Bellmer’s politics.
In his analysis of "Armored Bodies," Foster contrasts the Surrealist body with the Fascist body.
The Nazi aesthetic, exemplified by the official state art, fetishized the "armored" body: the male body as a seamless, rigid, impenetrable statue.
This body represented the solidity of the State, the purity of the Race, and the invulnerability of the Leader.
Bellmer’s Doll is the anti-armor.
It is soft, fragmented, permeable, and constantly falling apart.
It celebrates "degeneracy"—the very quality the Nazis sought to purge.
By presenting the body as a site of trauma, mutation, and fluid identity, Bellmer actively sabotaged the fascist ideal of wholeness.
The Doll is "indigestible" to fascism because it cannot be disciplined; its very structure is one of disobedience.
In 1937, the Nazis staged the infamous "Degenerate Art" (*Entartete Kunst*) exhibition, mocking modern art.
While Bellmer was not the primary target of this specific show (being less famous in Germany than the Expressionists), his work was spiritual kin to the "degeneracy" on display.
The Nazis viewed modernism as a symptom of racial and mental decay.
Bellmer embraced this "decay" as a form of resistance.
If the Nazis demanded a "healthy" body, Bellmer would give them a "diseased" one.
If the Nazis demanded a "productive" body, Bellmer would give them a useless one, devoted only to the non-productive expenditure of eroticism.
In 1938, a personal tragedy precipitated Bellmer’s final departure from Germany.
Bellmer's wife Margarete, who had been a conspirator in the Doll project (even helping to build the first one), died of tuberculosis.
With Margarete's death, the last tie to Berlin was severed.
Bellmer moved to Paris, taking the Doll (or parts of it) with him in a suitcase.

Upon arriving in Paris, Bellmer was immediately integrated into the planning for the *Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme* (International Surrealist Exhibition) of 1938, held at the Galerie Beaux-Arts.
This exhibition is legendary in art history for its immersive design by Marcel Duchamp (who hung coal sacks from the ceiling) and the "Street of Mannequins" in the hallway.
Bellmer was one of the artists invited to dress a mannequin for this street.

While many artists (like Masson and Dali) decorated their mannequins with found objects, Bellmer’s contribution was deeply consistent with his own practice, treating the mannequin as a site of violation and reconstruction.
The exhibition solidified Bellmer's status as the "master of the mannequin" within the group.
The outbreak of World War II in 1939 turned Bellmer from a celebrated guest into an "enemy alien."
Despite his anti-Nazi stance, Bellmer was a German citizen.
In 1939, Bellmer was arrested by the French authorities and interned at the Camp des Milles near Aix-en-Provence, a brick factory converted into a prison camp.
At Les Milles, Bellmer was interned alongside other German artists, including Max Ernst and Wols.
The conditions at Les Milles were difficult, but artistic production continued.
Bellmer drew at Les Milles, often using the brick architecture of the camp as a motif in his "anamorphic" portraits.
Bellmer was eventually released but lived in precarious conditions in the south of France before returning to Paris after the war.
After the war, Bellmer abandoned the construction of new Dolls, though he continued to photograph and draw them.
Bellmer shifted his focus to engraving and drawing, producing some of his most explicit work.
In 1947, Bellmer collaborated with Georges Bataille on a new edition of *Story of the Eye*.
The themes of *Story of the Eye*—the equivalencies between the eye, the egg, and the testicle—resonated perfectly with Bellmer’s anagrammatic logic.
In 1953, Bellmer met Unica Zurn, a German writer and artist.
Unica Zurn became Bellmer's partner and model.
Zurn’s practice of writing "anagram poems" paralleled Bellmer’s visual anagrams.
Bellmer photographed Zurn bound with string, creating the "Unica" series, which transformed the living flesh into sections resembling the articulated segments of the Doll.
Their relationship was intense and tragic, ending with Zurn’s suicide in 1970 and Bellmer’s decline until his death in 1975.
Bellmer’s work is not merely visual; it is a form of "corporeal philosophy."
Bellmer's major theoretical text, *Little Anatomy of the Physical Unconscious, or The Anatomy of the Image* (published in French in 1957), outlines the complex mechanics of his vision.
Bellmer argues that the body is governed by the "reflex."
When a specific part of the body experiences intense sensation (pain, sexual arousal), the body’s "center of gravity" shifts to that point.
If one has a toothache, the "ego" migrates to the tooth.
Bellmer calls this the creation of a "virtual center."
The Doll is an attempt to represent this invisible shifting of centers.
If the desire is focused on the leg, the leg becomes the whole body.
The "cephalopod" (head-leg creature) is a representation of a body where the brain (thought) is directly connected to the limb (action/flight/sex), bypassing the torso (digestion/heart).
Bellmer was fascinated by the linguistic coincidence that the French word *IMAGE* is an anagram of *MAGIE* (Magic).
Bellmer received a telegram from Man Ray pointing this out.
For Bellmer, the image was indeed a form of magic—a way of casting a spell on reality to make it conform to desire.
The Doll was a magical object, a totem used to ward off the reality of the father and the state, and to summon the "marvelous" into existence.
The legacy of *La Poupée* extends far beyond its Surrealist origins.
It is a foundational text for the "Post-Human" in art.
Cindy Sherman’s "Sex Pictures" (1992) and mannequin works clearly dialogue with Bellmer.
Like Bellmer, Cindy Sherman uses medical prosthetics and doll parts to construct grotesque, sexualized bodies that interrogate the "male gaze" while simultaneously inhabiting it.
Jake and Dinos Chapman’s *Zygotic Acceleration* (1995) features child mannequins fused together, with genitalia displaced to their faces.
This is a direct sculptural application of Bellmer’s anagrammatic theory—the displacement of the erogenous zone to create a "monstrous" new organism.

The image of the articulated, artificial girl has permeated pop culture, notably in Mamoru Oshii’s *Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence* (2004), which features dolls that are visual descendants of Bellmer’s creations.
Feminist reception of Bellmer has been divided.
Early critiques often viewed the Doll as a supreme example of misogyny—the literal objectification and dismemberment of the female body for male pleasure.
The violence of the images is undeniable.
However, scholars like Sue Taylor and Therese Lichtenstein have argued for a more complex reading.
They suggest that Bellmer *identifies* with the Doll.
The Doll is not "other"; it is a self-portrait.
Through the Doll, Bellmer explores his own passivity, his own castration anxiety, and his own desire to be "unmade" and "remade."
The Doll allows for a fluidity of gender where the male artist can inhabit the female form to escape the rigid expectations of masculinity (the "armored body") imposed by his father and the state.
Hans Bellmer’s *La Poupée* remains one of the most disturbing and intellectually rigorous projects of the 20th century.
It is a work that refuses to resolve itself.
It is at once a toy and a weapon, a love letter and a crime scene, a photograph and a sculpture.
By applying the engineer’s precision to the chaotic materials of the unconscious, Bellmer created a "mechanics of desire" that exposed the fragility of human identity.
The Doll demonstrates that the body is not a fixed fact, but a sentence waiting to be written—an anagram that can be scrambled to reveal the hidden demons and delights of the psyche.

In the shadow of the Holocaust and the total war of the 1930s and 40s, Bellmer’s dismantled mannequins stand as a silent, terrifying witness to the disintegration of the humanist subject, offering in its place a beauty that is, as Breton demanded, truly convulsive.

Hans Bellmer
============

In often violently erotic photographs and drawings, Hans Bellmer developed the Surrealist theme of mannequins and dolls as metaphors of sexuality with a singularly obsessive focus. He explored the usually pubescent female figure as fetish object. Bellmer's series _Die Puppe (The Doll)_, debuted in the 1934 issue of the Surrealist publication _Le Minotaure_, and the photographs were described as "variations on the assemblage of an articulated minor." The doll consisted of a wood-and-metal skeleton covered with a realistic body of plaster and papier mâché; a system of ball-joints allowed it to be shaped into endless disturbing configurations, appearing dismembered and monstrous.

Born in Katowice, Silesia, Bellmer worked in coal mines before entering the Berlin Technische Hochschule to study engineering in 1923. While there, he also studied perspective with George Grosz and established contact with Dada artists. From 1924 to 1936 he worked variously as a typographer and draftsman. He first made contact with the Surrealists in 1924 on a trip to Paris. In 1932 he was inspired by the opera _The Tales of Hoffmann_, and the next year collaborated on a production of Hoffmann's _The Sandman_: both works feature female automatons. At around this time, in opposition to the rise of Nazism, he stopped all work that supported the state. Bellmer began constructing his first "artificial girl" in 1934, with his wife, Margarete. Photographs of the doll were hand-colored by Bellmer for the first edition of his book _Die Puppe_. The second series of dolls, even more disarticulated than the first, were created in 1936-1938. Bellmer left Berlin in 1938 and settled in Paris where he was part of Surrealist circles. With the outbreak of the war, he was interned as a German citizen in a prison camp from 1940-1941. Bellmer's work appeared in numerous exhibitions, including the 1947 International Surrealist Exposition in Paris.

Lisa Soccio

Handy et al. _Reflections in a Glass Eye: Works from the International Center of Photography Collection_, New York: Bulfinch Press in association with the International Center of Photography, 1999, p. 208.
