35.title: Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme
35.content:
The **Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme** was an exhibition by [surrealist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") artists that took place from January 17 to February 24, 1938, in the generously equipped Galérie Beaux-Arts, run by [Georges Wildenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Wildenstein "Georges Wildenstein"), at 140, Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). It was organised by the French writer [André Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Breton "André Breton"), the surrealists' brain and theorist, and [Paul Éluard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_%C3%89luard "Paul Éluard"), the best known poet of the movement. The catalogue listed, along with the above, [Marcel Duchamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp") as generator and arbitrator (to appease the partly fierce conflicts mainly between Breton and Éluard), [Salvador Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") and [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst") as technical advisers, [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray") as head lighting technician and [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") as responsible for the design of the entrance and main hall with "water and foliage".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-blacksmith-1) The exhibition was staged in three sections, showing paintings and objects as well as unusually decorated rooms and [mannequins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannequin "Mannequin") which had been redesigned in various ways. With this holistic presentation of surrealist art work the movement wrote exhibition history.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-2)

[![Image 1: Building with storefronts and several levels of windows and balconies](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/140%2C_Rue_du_Faubourg_St._Honor%C3%A9.jpg/250px-140%2C_Rue_du_Faubourg_St._Honor%C3%A9.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:140,_Rue_du_Faubourg_St._Honor%C3%A9.jpg)

Built in 1860, the house at 140, Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré in Paris, in which exhibition was held. Photo taken in 2011

Before their first group exhibition in November 1925, which took place in Pierre Loeb's gallery "Pierre" in Paris, the surrealist artists had previously shown their works at solo exhibitions. The group exhibition showed works of [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico"), [Hans Arp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Arp "Hans Arp"), Max Ernst, [Paul Klee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Klee "Paul Klee"), [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray"), [André Masson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Masson "André Masson"), [Joan Miró](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Mir%C3%B3 "Joan Miró"), [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso") and [Pierre Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Roy_(artist)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pierre Roy (artist) (page does not exist)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-3) Another joint exhibition followed in 1928 in the Parisian gallery "Au Sacre du Printemps" with the title "Le Surréalisme, existe-t-il?" (Does [Surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") really exist?) Among the participants were Max Ernst, André Masson, Joan Miró, [Francis Picabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Picabia "Francis Picabia") und [Yves Tanguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Tanguy "Yves Tanguy"). Further group exhibitions followed. In 1931 the first surrealist exhibition in the US took place in the [Wadsworth Atheneum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadsworth_Atheneum "Wadsworth Atheneum") in [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut"), and in May 1936 the "Exposition surréaliste d'objets" was held in the Parisian gallery Charles Ratton, which particularly valued object art and also referred to [Primitivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitivism "Primitivism"), [sexual fetishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_fetishes "Sexual fetishes") and mathematical models.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-blacksmith-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-4)

In June of the same year the [International Surrealist Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Surrealist_Exhibition "International Surrealist Exhibition") was launched in the [New Burlington Galleries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Burlington_Galleries "New Burlington Galleries") in London. These exhibitions still made use of the usual form of representation, i.e. the White Room, which was designed at the "Sonderbund" exhibition in [Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne") in 1912. In 1938 however, André Breton wanted to establish a framework for the surrealist art in the [Beaux Arts Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux_Arts_Gallery "Beaux Arts Gallery"), in which the presentation itself was surrealist art.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-5) As a creative act it was to be a surreal experience, in which paintings and objects served as elements in a completely surrealist environment.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-6)

At the end of 1937, André Breton and [Nusch Éluard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nusch_%C3%89luard "Nusch Éluard") asked Duchamp to contribute ideas to the surrealist exhibition they were planning. Duchamp had already presented his works at previous exhibitions, but he never became a member because of his principle never to be part of any group. Nevertheless, Duchamp accepted the invitation to help design the exhibition. This led to cooperation on further projects, such as the First Papers of Surrealism exhibition, which took place in New York City in 1942.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-7) Various discreet meetings were held together with the inner circle of responsible curators and designers (Marcel Duchamp, Wolfgang Paalen, Man Ray, Max Ernst, Salvador Dalí) to discuss the general outlines and specific thematical questions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-8)

The catalogue and a reference book
----------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: The catalogue and a reference book")]

The eight-page catalogue, in which all the artists were listed in huge capital letters and so impossible to overlook, provided information about the people involved in the exhibition. André Breton and Paul Éluard acted as organisers, Marcel Duchamp was named as "Generateur-arbitre", Salvador Dalí and Max Ernst were listed as technical directors, Man Ray was chief lighting technician and Wolfgang Paalen responsible for "water and foliage".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-blacksmith-1)

Accompanying the exhibition, the gallery of Beaux-Arts published in addition to the catalogue a 76-page _Dictionnaire abrégé du surréalisme_ under the direction of Breton and Éluard. It was a dictionary of Surrealism with an introduction by the French art critic and artistic director of the gallery, Raymond Congniat, along with cover artwork by Yves Tanguy and an illustrated section which was quite extensive for the time and which summed up the proof of origin of the complete surrealistic artwork. Here, all artists' names, "all keywords, all obsessional concepts and motives, the new inspirational image techniques and the ancestors"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-9) were unified.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-10) The names and terms from "Absurde" to "Zen" and "Zibou", organized in alphabetical order, were mostly explained by quotations from publications written by representative members of the surrealist movement.

The exhibition was divided into three parts: a "lobby" with the _taxi pluvieux_ (rain cab) by [Salvador Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") and two main sections; the first the _Plus belles rues de Paris_ ("The most beautiful streets of Paris") with surrealistically fitted mannequins rented from a French manufacturer, and a central room arranged by [Marcel Duchamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp") and [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") with lighting by Man Ray. Paintings, collages, photographs and graphics hung - poorly lit - on the walls and on Duchamp's two revolving doors. [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") created an artificial pond with real waterlillies and reed, covered the whole floor of the exhibition (including the entrance pathway with wet leaves and mud from the Monparnasse cemetery, and installed his objects "Chaise envahie de lierre" and [Nuage articulé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuage_articul%C3%A9 "Nuage articulé").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-11) Further objects were placed on different kinds of pedestals. Using objects and items from nature and civilization, the room itself was "transformed into a gloomy-absurd ambience: less exhibition room than cave and womb."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-12)

[![Image 2: Advertisement for the International Exhibition of Surrealism at the Beaux-Arts Gallery in Paris](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Exposition_surrealisme_Paris_1938_carton.jpg/250px-Exposition_surrealisme_Paris_1938_carton.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Exposition_surrealisme_Paris_1938_carton.jpg)

Invitation card depicting _Enigmarelle_

The exhibition was opened late on the first night, at 10 pm. Evening dress was required and all manner of highlights had been promised: hysteria, a sky full of flying dogs and the presence of [Enigmarelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigmarelle "Enigmarelle"), an humanoid [automaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automaton "Automaton"), a descendant of [Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenstein "Frankenstein").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-blacksmith-1) Marcel Duchamp could not attend the exhibition, because he and his partner Mary Reynolds had gone to London in order to select and hang paintings and drawings by [Jean Cocteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Cocteau "Jean Cocteau") for [Peggy Guggenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Guggenheim "Peggy Guggenheim")'s _Gallery Guggenheim Jeune_. The gallery was opened on January 24, 1938, with a Jean Cocteau exhibition.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-13) Also not present were Joan Miró and Yves Tanguy, who did not usually attend collaborative events, as well as [René Magritte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte "René Magritte"), who lived in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-blacksmith-1) At Ernst, Dalí and Paalen had trained the actress [Hélène Vanel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9l%C3%A8ne_Vanel "Hélène Vanel") to do a performance. She jumped out of pillows lying on the floor with chains wrapped around her naked body. After splashing wildly in [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen")´s puddle she reappeared dressed in a tattered evening dress a short time later "and gave a very realistic performance of a hysterical attack" in one of the beds in the main hall.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-14)

The event showed 229 works by 60 exhibitors from 14 countries[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-15) and contained paintings, art objects, [collages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage "Collage"), photographs and [installations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Installation_art "Installation art"). Artists and writers like [Hans Bellmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Bellmer "Hans Bellmer"), [Leonora Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonora_Carrington "Leonora Carrington"), [Joseph Cornell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Cornell "Joseph Cornell") and [Óscar Domínguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93scar_Dom%C3%ADnguez "Óscar Domínguez") participated. [Salvador Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") was represented with six paintings, among which was "[The Great Masturbator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Masturbator "The Great Masturbator")" from 1929. [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") showed his painting "Paysage totémique de mon enfance" among others, as well as his objects "Le moi et le soi", "Potènce avec paratonnerre" (a life-sized gibbet with a lightning rod dedicated to the German philosopher [Georg Christoph Lichtenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Christoph_Lichtenberg "Georg Christoph Lichtenberg"). Paalen's umbrella made with sponges [Nuage articulé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuage_articul%C3%A9 "Nuage articulé") was hanging from the ceiling.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-16) The "Ultra-furniture", 1937, by [Kurt Seligmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Seligmann "Kurt Seligmann"), sculptures by [Alberto Giacometti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Giacometti "Alberto Giacometti"), and objects by [Meret Oppenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meret_Oppenheim "Meret Oppenheim"), including "Breakfast in Fur" from 1936, were presented along with five other works, such as "La Baguerre d'Austerlitz" and a replica of the [Ready-mades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Found_object "Found object") "Bottle Dryer" by [Marcel Duchamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp"). Furthermore, there were 14 pictures by [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst"), such as "The Rendezvous of Friends" from 1922 and "The Triumph of Surrealism" from 1937; works by [Stanley William Hayter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_William_Hayter "Stanley William Hayter"), [Georges Hugnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Hugnet "Georges Hugnet"), [Humphrey Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Jennings "Humphrey Jennings"), and [Léo Malet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9o_Malet "Léo Malet"); "The Expectation", 1936, by [Richard Oelze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Oelze "Richard Oelze"); and two surrealistic pictures by [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso"). [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray") presented, among other works, "A l'heure de l'observatoire – les amoureux", 1932–34, as well as "Irrlichter" from 1932 to 1937. There were nine works by [René Magritte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte "René Magritte"), for example "The Key to the Fields" from 1936 and "The Therapist II" from 1937; eight early pictures by [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico"); works by [André Masson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Masson "André Masson") and [Roberto Matta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Matta "Roberto Matta"); and several works by [Joan Miró](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Mir%C3%B3 "Joan Miró"), including "Dutch Interior I" from 1928. Other artists represented included [Roland Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Penrose "Roland Penrose"); [Jindřich Štyrský](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jind%C5%99ich_%C5%A0tyrsk%C3%BD "Jindřich Štyrský"); [Yves Tanguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Tanguy "Yves Tanguy") with nine pictures, among which was "From the Other Side of the Bridge" from 1936; [Toyen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyen "Toyen"); [Raoul Ubac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Ubac "Raoul Ubac"); and [Remedios Varo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remedios_Varo "Remedios Varo").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-17) And the Danish painter [Rita Kernn-Larsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Kernn-Larsen "Rita Kernn-Larsen") with her self-portrait " Know Thyself."

Dalí's Rain Taxi, a former taxi, welcomed the visitors in the forecourt. The old automobile was covered with ivy inside and out, and a female dummy with dishevelled hair and dressed in an [evening gown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_gown "Evening gown") sat between some heads of lettuce and [chicory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicory "Chicory") in the back of the car. Next to her was a [sewing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewing_machine "Sewing machine"). The driver was a doll, whose head was framed by the mouth of a shark and whose eyes were covered by a pair of dark glasses. The interior was constantly sprayed with water so that the clothes of the lady were drenched and the blond wig dissolved into felted strands, while some edible snails, visible on the lady's neck, left their slimy traces.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-nils-18)

In 1974, Dalí exhibited his Rain Taxi in his birthplace of [Figueres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figueres "Figueres") in [Catalonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia"), in the inner courtyard of the museum for the opening of the [Theatre-Museu Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dal%C3%AD_Theatre_and_Museum "Dalí Theatre and Museum"). The roof of the taxi was decorated with the large sculpture _Esther_ by [Ernst Fuchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Fuchs_(artist) "Ernst Fuchs (artist)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-19)

### The most beautiful streets in Paris

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: The most beautiful streets in Paris")]

From the forecourt the visitors passed into a long corridor with street signs. In the _Plus belles rue de Paris_ artists such as Marcel Duchamp, Max Ernst, Joan Miró, Man Ray, André Masson, Yves Tanguy and Wolfgang Paalen exhibited dummies, provocatively designed and dressed as sex objects and standing in front of the street signs. The sixteen figures showed surrealist motives and techniques, which consisted of concealment and revelation, and expressed captivated [lust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lust "Lust"), the power of unconscious desire and the breaking of [taboos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo "Taboo").

The street signs partly referred to surrealistic obsessions and sometimes had a fictionally poetic character, but also actual street names, such as Rue Nicolas-Flamel in Paris, were also used. This name was a dedication to the medieval alchemist [Nicolas Flamel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Flamel "Nicolas Flamel"), whose works were cited by [André Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Breton "André Breton"), [Paul Éluard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_%C3%89luard "Paul Éluard") and [Robert Desnos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Desnos "Robert Desnos") as examples of surrealistic poetry. The Surrealists owe their mission statement of the sewing machine and the umbrella on the dissection table to the writer [Lautréamont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lautr%C3%A9amont "Lautréamont"), who lived in the Rue Vivienne. [18] According to [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst"), two or more "alien elements provoke the highest poetical lightning" when they meet on a grid which is foreign to them.[19] The Panorama Passage referred to one of the Surrealists' favorite places in Paris, the Rue de la Vielle Lanterne, in memory of the street, which no longer exists. In this street [Gérard de Nerval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9rard_de_Nerval "Gérard de Nerval"), who, according to Breton, was the role model for the movement, committed suicide. The Porte de Lilas referred to La Closerie de Lilas - the meeting place of the [intellectuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual "Intellectual"). Other street names were mystifying inventions, like the Rue de la Transfusion ([Blood Transfusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_Transfusion "Blood Transfusion") Street) and the Rue de Tous les Diables (Devil's Street).[20]

Masson's mannequin attracted great attention because he had squeezed its head into a [bird cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_cage "Bird cage") covered with red fish made of [celluloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celluloid "Celluloid"). It was gagged with a ribbon made of [velvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet "Velvet"), with a [pansy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pansy "Pansy") placed at its mouth. Underneath, red [paprika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paprika "Paprika") caught in traps grew out of a ground of coarse salt grains. The paprika pointed upwards to the mannequin's [genitalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genitalia "Genitalia"), like many tiny [erections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erection "Erection"). [Marcel Duchamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp") dressed his mannequin in a man's felt hat, shirt, tie and jacket; a red bulb blinked in the breast pocket, and the lower part of the mannequin was naked - "Rose Selavy (Duchamp's alter ego) in one of her provocative and androgynous moods". [Yves Tanguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Tanguy "Yves Tanguy") draped it with [phallus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phallus "Phallus")-like spindles, [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray") arranged his figure with big [tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tears "Tears") and decorated its head with [pitch pipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_pipe "Pitch pipe") and glass balloons. [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") used [mushrooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushroom "Mushroom") and [moss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moss "Moss") to give his mannequin an overgrown look, and added a giant [vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire")-like [bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat "Bat"); [Óscar Domínguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93scar_Dom%C3%ADnguez "Óscar Domínguez") placed an enormous [siphon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siphon "Siphon") at the side of his mannequin. Out of the siphon an abundant jet of drapery was fired out. At the feet of his "Black Widow", [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst") set a man with a lion head, lying on the floor and sprinkled with paint. He intended to place a glowing bulb in her underwear, exposed by her pulled-up skirt, but Breton prevented this. Only at second glance were the visitors able to realise that they were looking at "artificial" women.

_The most beautiful streets of Paris_ led to the main room. It was designed by Duchamp and Paalen in the form of a [grotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grotto "Grotto") or womb, with 1200 coal bags hanging from the ceiling, filled with newspapers instead of coal. Despite this, evil-smelling coal dust trickled down. They resembled modern [stalactites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalactite "Stalactite"), which inverted the categories of up and down. Paalen's installation "Avant La Mare" with pond, water lilies and reed, as well as his floor decoration with dead leaves and mud turned the whole atmosphere into a sphere of humidity, fog and romantic twilight, especially since Man Ray's lighting through [soffits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soffit "Soffit") did not work out on the evening of the [vernissage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernissage "Vernissage") visitors were forced to use the [flashlights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashlight "Flashlight") that were handed out in order to orient themselves in the darkness. Frequently visitors forgot to bring them back. [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray") later remarked: "Unnecessary to mention that the flashlights were pointed at the faces of the people rather than at the artworks themselves. As at every overcrowded vernissage, everyone wanted to know who else was around." Some of the historians see the design of the main hall as a metaphor for the menaced situation of surrealism, mirrored in the harassment of the political situation before the war,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-20) as well as an outsized uterus as vade mecum against the deeper reasons for the crisis, which would originate in the paternalistic fixations of the whole epoch. Especially the biographer of [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen"), [Andreas Neufert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Neufert "Andreas Neufert"), represents the latter reading and wants to see the installation as a whole as symptom for an ideological shift inside surrealism away from [Sigmund Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmund_Freud "Sigmund Freud")´s rigid interpretation of the [Oedipus complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oedipus_complex "Oedipus complex") towards [Otto Rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Rank "Otto Rank")´s theory of [The Trauma of Birth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Trauma_of_Birth "The Trauma of Birth") with its recognition of the emotional nature of the child and its ties to the mother, which was represented at this time exclusively by [Wolfgang Paalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Paalen "Wolfgang Paalen") and his wife, the poet [Alice Rahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Rahon "Alice Rahon").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-21)

Contemporary reception
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Contemporary reception")]

The Exposition Internationale du Surréalism was a major cultural event which drew throngs of visitors. On the opening night, more than 3,000 people came to see the exhibition. Sometimes the jostling was so intense that the police had to take action. However, over the following days the exhibition, which was hyped as a spectacle, averaged more than 500 people per day. The exhibition attracted a mostly [bourgeois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeois "Bourgeois") audience, among which were many foreigners: "[The opening] was attended by the whole Parisian elite as well as a remarkable number of beautiful American women, German Jews and crazy old women from England [...] Never before have so many of the high society stepped on each other's toes [...]."

Before the opening, Raymond Cogniat had explicitly announced to the press that there would be an atmosphere of trepidation: "It is an ascension to a mysterious world, where the [burlesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlesque "Burlesque") has less of a place than trepidation; where the laughing of the visitors covers up their inner unease; where even their anger lays bare their defeat. Surrealism is no game, it is obsession." The effect they hoped for reached only a few visitors; only in rare cases did anyone report having a "feeling of unease, of [claustrophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claustrophobia "Claustrophobia") and the premonition of a terrible calamity", as Marie-Louise Fermet wrote in _La Lumière_. In _Le Figaro littéraire_, Jean Fraysee reported a simultaneous occurring of uncertainty, [melancholia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melancholia "Melancholia") and [black humour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_humour "Black humour") in the atmosphere – and so confirmed that the aims of the exhibitors had been reached.

However, the press strongly disapproved of the surrealist artists' "forced lunacy" [35], stating that the exhibition merely offered a "collection of sad jokes"[36]. Many journalists admitted that their reaction to the exhibits had been laughter, not as a means of hiding their fear but rather because they were reminded of a "carnival"[37]. A lot of reports also emphasized the exhibition's alleged harmlessness and denounced surrealism as "art without danger"[38]. The French magazine _Paris Midi_ judged that the [surrealists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") were no longer "enfants terribles", but rather "a group of nice boys" working in a "nostalgic and immature"[39] manner. Art historian Annabelle Görgen considered these reactions to contain "too much [polemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemic "Polemic") to be taken as an expression of reserved amusement [...]. In fact, the laughter represented a defensive stance at least against the [alogical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic "Logic")."[40] In the end, she saw the newspapers' scathing criticism as a success for the surrealists since the artists explicitly wanted to evoke the kind of anger that had manifested itself in the reviews.

Most critics derided individual objects, thereby missing the point of the holistic concept of the exhibition. Even less prejudiced commentators such as Josef Breitenbach, one of the photographers who elaborately documented the exhibition, praised individual installations without getting anything out of the exhibition as a whole. He highly valued works by Duchamp, de Chirico, Miró, Ernst and others, but nevertheless summarised the exhibition as a "salad of exaggeratedness and bad taste".[41] This harsh judgment serves as an example for the fact that the innovative part of the exhibition, holistic production, was not recognized by contemporaries.

Impact on art history
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Impact on art history")]

Our knowledge of the exhibition is mainly conveyed by numerous photographs, such as works by [Raoul Ubac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Ubac "Raoul Ubac"), [Josef Breitenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Breitenbach "Josef Breitenbach"), Robert Valencay, [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray"), [Denise Bellon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_Bellon "Denise Bellon") and Thérèse Le Prat, who generally not only dealt with surrealistic mannequins in single pictures but in entire sequences.[15] In 1966 Man Ray documented the exhibition in a book. It was published as a limited edition in Paris by Jean Petithory with the title, "Résurrection des mannequins in Paris by Jean Petithory". Apart from an explanatory essay, the book contains fifteen silver-gelatine photograph prints.

### The mannequin as an object of art

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: The mannequin as an object of art")]

The surrealist artists had a special interest in mannequins. With these mannequins the art myth of [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid "Ovid")'s [Pygmalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmalion_(mythology) "Pygmalion (mythology)"), a sculptor who carved the perfect woman, fell in love with her and then asked [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus") to awaken her to life, is kept alive. [Raoul Hausmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Hausmann "Raoul Hausmann"), who was an artist of [Dadaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dada "Dada"), which preceded [Surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism"), had already created a mechanical head in 1919 named "The Spirit of Our Age". It was a decorated head of [papier-mâché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papier-m%C3%A2ch%C3%A9 "Papier-mâché"), such as [hairdresser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairdresser "Hairdresser") apprentices use to learn how to make [wigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wig "Wig"). Thus, the everyday item lost its common function and experienced a transformation into an artistic concept. Hausmann was involved in the first international Dada exhibition, which took place in 1920 in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"). The sculptor and photographer [Hans Bellmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Bellmer "Hans Bellmer"), who emigrated to Paris in 1938, was also a participant of the exhibition. He had been experimenting with mannequins since the beginning of the 1930s.

At the beginning of 2011 an exhibition called "surreal things" in the [Schirn Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schirn_Art_Gallery "Schirn Art Gallery") in [Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt "Frankfurt") showcased not only sculptures and objects from [Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") to [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray"), but also documentary photographs of mannequins from [Raoul Ubac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Ubac "Raoul Ubac") and Denise Bellon. According to the Schirn art gallery, the objects testify to "the passion of the [Surrealists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") for the iconography of the mannequin and reflect the desire to sexualise the body by means of surrealistic methods, such as combinatorics, veiling and exposure."

### The exhibition as a final manifestation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: The exhibition as a final manifestation")]

[![Image 3: Salvador Dali, in a black-and-white photo, looks back over his left shoulder with a floral design behind him](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD_1939.jpg/250px-Salvador_Dal%C3%AD_1939.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salvador_Dal%C3%AD_1939.jpg)

[Salvador Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") in 1939. Photographer: [Carl van Vechten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_van_Vechten "Carl van Vechten")

Intentionally or not, the exhibition in 1938 turned out to be the last highlight and final manifestation of the surrealist movement. It had concentrated once again all of its energy in order to affirm its significance and potential for provocation. Political circumstances as well as personal, politically motivated differences (for example in 1938 between [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Breton "André Breton") and [Éluard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_%C3%89luard "Paul Éluard"), who sympathized with [Stalinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalinism "Stalinism")), led Éluard to leave the group of surrealists. [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst") and [Man Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_Ray "Man Ray") followed suit out of solidarity [47]. The final break between Breton and Dalí followed in 1939, which sealed the temporary end of the surrealist community. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") many artists went into exile in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"); their influence played a decisive role in future styles of art such as [abstract expressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_expressionism "Abstract expressionism"), [Neo-Dada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Dada "Neo-Dada") and [Pop Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Art "Pop Art") [48]. In 1942, Breton and Duchamp, who had emigrated from France, organized the exhibition "First Papers of Surrealism" alongside [Sidney Janis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Janis "Sidney Janis") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") [49].

When Breton and Duchamp opened the exhibition "Le surréalisme en 1947" in the [Galerie Maeght](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerie_Maeght "Galerie Maeght") in Paris after the war, Breton referred back to the exhibition of 1938. He remarked that, on the one hand, the exhibition was supposed to represent the surrealist intention, which was situated on the boundary between poetry and reality, while, on the other hand, it was also supposed to manifest the spirit of 1938. According to Breton's biographer, [Volker Zotz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volker_Zotz "Volker Zotz"), the exhibition of 1947 did not, however, have the same effect as its Parisian forerunner in 1938 and was criticised for being too exclusive. He described post-war Surrealism as an "esoteric circle", while many pieces which had their origin in its roots had achieved world-wide recognition. Duchamp's biographer, [Calvin Tomkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Tomkins "Calvin Tomkins"), described the exhibition as "the movement's last hurrah". He remarked that the post-war era had found different outlets, namely [existentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism") in Europe and [abstract expressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_expressionism "Abstract expressionism") in the United States.

### Influence on exhibitions since the 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Influence on exhibitions since the 1960s")]

The rejection of modernist, white-walled galleries and the _[mise-en-scène](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mise-en-sc%C3%A8ne "Mise-en-scène")_, as well as the placing of equal emphasis on works of art and finds was a decisive forerunner of exhibitions and installations of the 1960s. In 1962, the Dylaby (dynamic labyrinth) exhibition at the [Stedelijk Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stedelijk_Museum "Stedelijk Museum") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") built directly on the 1938 exhibition. Involved in Dylaby were [Jean Tinguely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Tinguely "Jean Tinguely"), [Daniel Spoerri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Spoerri "Daniel Spoerri"), [Robert Rauschenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rauschenberg "Robert Rauschenberg"), [Martial Raysse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_Raysse "Martial Raysse"), [Niki de Saint Phalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niki_de_Saint_Phalle "Niki de Saint Phalle"), Per Olof Ultvedt, and its organiser [Pontus Hultén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontus_Hult%C3%A9n "Pontus Hultén").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Internationale_du_Surr%C3%A9alisme#cite_note-EFPDeath-22) The room and exhibition as part of the artwork established itself as "a medium unto itself within the medium of the exhibition, which emerged out of surrealist practice." Among the exhibitors that helped, "based on surrealist practice, to establish the exhibition as a medium", was the BEUYS exhibition by the sculptor [Joseph Beuys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Beuys "Joseph Beuys") at the [Abteiberg Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abteiberg_Museum "Abteiberg Museum") in [Mönchengladbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6nchengladbach "Mönchengladbach"), Germany (Sept-Oct 1967), along with '503 (1600 Cubic Feet) Level Dirt' by [Walter De Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_De_Maria "Walter De Maria") (Sept-Oct 1968) at the [Heiner Friedrich Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiner_Friedrich_Gallery "Heiner Friedrich Gallery") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), and 'Senza titolo (Dodici cavelli vivi)' by [Jannis Kounellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jannis_Kounellis "Jannis Kounellis"), who, in 1969, put twelve lively horses on display at the Galleria L'Attico in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"). As a result, the exhibitions of the 1980s emerged.

From March to May 1995 the [Ubu gallery](https://web.archive.org/web/20120121095913/http://www.ubugallery.com/phpwcms/?id=34,162,0,0,1,0) in New York, which was founded just the year before, paid homage to the ground-breaking 1938 exhibition. Exhibits, photographs and Duchamp's installation from the main room were shown.

The Wilhelm-Hack museum in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen") presented another retrospective in the context of their exhibition with the title _Gegen jede Vernunft. Surrealismus Paris-Prag im Jahr 2009/10_ ("Against all reason. Surrealism Paris-Prague in 2009/10"). Exhibited was a partial reproduction: the main room as decorated by Marcel Duchamp featured sacks of coal mounted on the ceiling, leaves on the floor, a [brazier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazier "Brazier") and a bed, as well as paintings on the wall. An audio track filled the room with the sounds of marching soldiers and hysterical laughter. Just as in 1938 the visitors were forced to explore the room with a flashlight.

The Fondation Beyeler in [Riehen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riehen "Riehen") near [Basel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basel "Basel") showed the first comprehensive surrealist exhibition in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") from October 2, 2011, until January 29, 2012. The visitors were guided through the exhibition, as in 1938, by imitation Parisian street signs with fictitious or real names. The title of the exhibition is _Dalí, Magritte, Miró - Surrealismus in Paris_ ("Dalí, Magritte, Miró - Surrealism in Paris").

Entry catalogue A dream collection - Surrealism in Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Author: Marijke Peyser In February 1935 Hans Bellmer spent a short time in Paris, where he got to know André Breton and other Surrealists, including Paul Éluard and Henri Parisot. From then on, Bellmer’s work was included in the Surrealists’ exhibitions. In the same year he made a second version of the doll with greater flexibility than the original doll he made in 1934. She had arms, two pairs of legs, four spherical breasts, three pelvises and a torso complete with female genitalia that could be assembled in all manner of ways. The doll also had her own extensive wardrobe, wigs and shoes. This doll played the leading role in _Les jeux de la poupée_, which was published in 1949. As there was in _Die Puppe__,_ which was made in 1934, there is an accompanying text. In 1934 Bellmer himself wrote an introduction headed ‘Erinnerungen zum Thema Puppe’: in 1949 the photos were accompanied by fourteen poems by Éluard and, again, an introductory essay by Bellmer, ‘Notes au sujet de la jointure a boule’, a pseudo-scientific discourse he wrote in 1938 and translated into French with the Surrealist poet and artist Georges Hugnet in 1946.[\[1\]](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/118762/les-jeux-de-la-poupee#_ftn1) Along with Éluard, friends like Raoul Haussmann and Christian d’Orgeix helped Bellmer to colour the photographs by hand.[\[2\]](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/118762/les-jeux-de-la-poupee#_ftn2) A hundred and forty-two copies were published. In 2002 Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen purchased number 109. Each photograph in _Les jeux de la poupée_ tells a story. The doll is usually shown in a domestic setting, for example in a bedroom, a kitchen, on stairs or in a cellar. The atmosphere of the photographs is perverted and menacing: a carpet-beater indicates that the doll will get a beating or has already been hit; other photographs show her hanging on a hook or the parts of her dismantled body left like rubbish on stairs. Torture threatens or has already happened. It is dangerous outside as well: a bloodied doll is watched by a voyeur hiding behind a tree. The viewer is part of a cruel world, created by the artist, where the tormentor remains unseen. What we do see is the ‘foreplay’ or the result of the tortures the doll has undergone.[\[3\]](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/118762/les-jeux-de-la-poupee#_ftn3) Bellmer’s disturbing, erotic manipulations of the doll were the starting point for the artist Cindy Sherman’s ‘Sex Pictures’ (c. 1992), one of which, _[Untitled # 258](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/4721/untitled-258),_ is in Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen’s collection. In this series of photographs she reacts to the visual imagery and conventions of the Surrealists, whereas Bellmer in his turn was campaigning against the Aryan ideal type of the healthy, fertile woman in his photographic series about the damage to the girl’s body.[\[4\]](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/118762/les-jeux-de-la-poupee#_ftn4) In a departure from her other work, Sherman did not pose for the ‘Sex Pictures’ herself, but used parts from plastic dolls that had clearly been very badly treated, comparable to Bellmer’s photographs. Unlike Bellmer’s pictures, however they never become truly disturbing. [Show research A dream collection - Surrealism in Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/research/a-dream-collection-surrealism-in-museum-boijmans-van-beuningen) [Show catalogue entry Hide catalogue entry](https://www.boijmans.nl/en/collection/artworks/118762/les-jeux-de-la-poupee#) All about the artist -------------------- ### Hans Bellmer #### Katowice 1902 - Parijs 1975 The artist Hans Bellmer, originally from Poland, published anonymous photographs of his dolls in the book 'Die Puppe' (the doll) in 1934. La Poupée


=============

[Hans Bellmer](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Hans+Bellmer&searchField=ArtistCulture) German, born Poland

1936

Not on view

In his nightmarish tableaux of mutilated and reassembled dolls posed in domestic interiors, Bellmer grappled with the base condition of the human body and with the bodily fragment as fetish object. Mannequins and dolls—simultaneously familiar and strange—supplied the material for his primal expressions of terror and awe, which often evoked the innocent violence and latent sexuality of childhood games. Whether they are read as Freudian emblems of the uncanny or as ominous harbingers of Nazi atrocities, Bellmer’s images exemplify the Surrealist view of the female body as the source of simultaneous fascination and revulsion.

Cramer](https://smarthistory.org/author/dr-charles-cramer/ "Posts by Dr. Charles Cramer") and [Dr. Kim Grant](https://smarthistory.org/author/dr-kim-grant/ "Posts by Dr. Kim Grant") [![Image 23: Galerie Surréaliste, c. 1927, photo by Man Ray](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Galerie.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Galerie.jpg) Galerie Surréaliste, c. 1927, photo by Man Ray Surrealism was the first modern art movement to make the creation and design of exhibitions a major focus of its activity. The group transformed the art exhibition from a traditional display of artworks into a staged venue intended to provoke new ideas and experiences. The contents of Surrealist exhibitions were typically eclectic and included works by Surrealist artists, other artists and non-artists admired by the Surrealists, as well as objects of various sorts and artifacts from cultures perceived as “[primitive](https://smarthistory.org/primitivism-and-modern-art/).” ### Exhibitions as Surrealist experiences From the beginning, Surrealist exhibitions were intended to provide a Surrealist experience for viewers and lead them to perform their own acts of Surrealist imagination. The juxtaposition of disparate works and objects in the extended space of an exhibition would, it was hoped, provoke the creation of a new world, using the same mechanism as that employed in a [Surrealist collage](https://smarthistory.org/surrealist-techniques-collage/). [![Image 24: Man Ray exhibition card](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/4ae3f146c0f7050917c41b425f3848a3-idea-man-man-ray.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/4ae3f146c0f7050917c41b425f3848a3-idea-man-man-ray.jpg) Man Ray exhibition card During the 1920s the Surrealists ran their own art gallery, which staged several unconventional exhibitions. Man Ray’s work was exhibited with art from Oceanic cultures, while Tanguy’s paintings were paired with Native American works. These non-European works were also seen as products of unconscious thinking, and as such fully equal to the works of Surrealist artists in providing insight into the immense creative resources of the arational mind. ### Contempt for art market values [![Image 25: Left: Exquisite Corpse drawing by Yves Tanguy, Joan Miró, Max Morise, and Man Ray, 1927, ink and pencil on paper, 14 1/8 x 9 inches (MoMA); Right: Exquisite Corpse drawing by Yves Tanguy, André Breton, Max Morise, and Man Ray, c. 1927](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/EC-2.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/EC-2.jpg) Left: Exquisite Corpse drawing by Yves Tanguy, Joan Miró, Max Morise, and Man Ray, 1927, ink and pencil on paper, 14 1/8 x 9 inches (MoMA); Right: Exquisite Corpse drawing by Yves Tanguy, André Breton, Max Morise, and Man Ray, c. 1927 The Surrealist Gallery also presented an exhibition of “exquisite corpse” drawings. These are drawings of figures made by a collaboration of three to five people using a method derived from parlor games. Each person draws part of the body and then folds the paper over so the person drawing the next section cannot see the previous drawing. Once the figure is completed the paper is unfolded and the strange juxtapositions of the various parts become a new Surrealist entity. The “exquisite corpse” method demonstrated many basic Surrealist principles.Both artists and non-artists participated in the making of exquisite corpses, which, like all Surrealist works, were not intended to be the result of artistic skill. The group nature of the drawings as well as their arbitrary automatic creation were intended to subvert any attempt to exalt the individual artist and his or her talent. These are drawings anyone can do. The exhibition of exquisite corpse drawings in the Surrealist Gallery demonstrated the group’s contempt for conventional assumptions about the value of art and the skills of artists that underpin the art market. ### Irrational categories of display [![Image 26: Surrealist Objects exhibition at Galerie Charles Ratton, 1936](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Surrealist-Objects.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Surrealist-Objects.jpg) Surrealist Objects exhibition at Galerie Charles Ratton, 1936 The Surrealist Gallery did not survive very long, but the Surrealists continued to stage exhibitions, which grew in scope and ambition during the 1930s. The Surrealist Exhibition of Objects was held in the gallery of Charles Ratton, a dealer in African, Oceanic, and Native American arts. This 1936 exhibition brought together over two hundred objects divided into categories, including [Surrealist objects](https://smarthistory.org/meret-oppenheim-object-fur-covered-cup-saucer-and-spoon/) as well as natural objects, interpreted objects, mathematical objects, found objects, readymade objects, and so-called [“savage” objects](https://smarthistory.org/primitivism-and-modern-art/) (the art of Oceania and Native Americans). [![Image 27: Surrealist Objects exhibition at Galerie Charles Ratton, 1936](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Surrealist-Objects-2.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Surrealist-Objects-2.jpg) Surrealist Objects exhibition at Galerie Charles Ratton, 1936 The eclectic presentation brought together objects typically exhibited in very different contexts: art galleries, natural history museums, anthropological museums, science museums, and flea markets. By upsetting the conventional categories of knowledge and presenting an alternative, illogical system, the Surrealists demonstrated how context creates meaning. The exhibition undermined the supposedly rational divisions of human knowledge using irrational strategies of display. ### Surrealist environments The most famous Surrealist exhibition was the 1938 International Exhibition of Surrealism at the Beaux Arts Gallery in Paris. It displayed 300 works and objects by over sixty artists from fifteen different countries. The scale of the exhibition was impressive, and its installation design made it truly remarkable. Visitors were enfolded in an entire Surrealist environment. [![Image 28: Roger Schall, Untitled (International Surrealist Exhibition, Paris), 1938, gelatin silver print, 22.1 x 21.1 cm (MoMA)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Schall.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Schall.jpg) Roger Schall, _Untitled (International Surrealist Exhibition, Paris)_, 1938, gelatin silver print, 22.1 x 21.1 cm (MoMA) In the lobby was Dalí’s _Rainy Taxi_, an old car surrounded by vines and installed with a system of tubing that created a downpour in the interior. Two mannequins, one with a shark’s head and one with a woman’s, sat inside surrounded by lettuce and covered in live snails. [![Image 29: Left: Man Ray, André Masson’s mannequin at the International Surrealist Exhibition, 1938; Right: Man Ray, Joan Miró’s mannequin at the International Surrealist Exhibition, 1938](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Masson-and-Miro.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Masson-and-Miro.jpg) Left: Man Ray, André Masson’s mannequin at the International Surrealist Exhibition, 1938; Right: Man Ray, Joan Miró’s mannequin at the International Surrealist Exhibition, 1938 Leading from the lobby was a long hallway lined by twenty mannequins, each costumed by a Surrealist artist. At the end of the passageway was the main hall of the exhibition, designed by [Marcel Duchamp](https://smarthistory.org/art-as-concept-duchamp/). The ceiling was hung with hundreds of sacks of coal, while the floor was covered with dead leaves and had a pool with water lilies and reeds. In the center of the room was an old iron heater, and in each corner were large beds covered in satin quilts. [![Image 30: Roger Schall, Untitled (International Surrealist Exhibition, Paris), 1938, gelatin silver print, 22.1 x 21.1 cm (MoMA)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Schall-2.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Schall-2.jpg) Roger Schall, _Untitled (International Surrealist Exhibition, Paris)_, 1938, gelatin silver print, 22.1 x 21.1 cm (MoMA) Paintings were hung on the walls as well as on two revolving doors next to the heater. Surrealist furniture and objects were displayed throughout. The room was unlit, and visitors were given flashlights to use during their journey through the exhibition. During opening night a German military march was played through a loudspeaker, coffee was roasted to emanate the “perfumes of Brazil,” and a dancer performed a dance titled “The Unconsummated Act” in and around the pool. For the most part art critics mocked the exhibition, but it was an enormous popular success. [![Image 31: First Papers of Surrealism exhibition, 1942](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/First-Papers-of-Surrealism-exhibition.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/First-Papers-of-Surrealism-exhibition.jpg) First Papers of Surrealism exhibition, 1942 The elaborate installation of the 1938 exhibition was not repeated, but in 1942 Duchamp designed another installation for the First Papers of Surrealism Exhibition in New York City. He wound a mile of string into a labyrinth that covered the walls and art works like an enormous spider web. Visitors were literally enmeshed with the Surrealist works in the environment. The illogical space he created seemed to be more a physical manifestation of mental space than an environment to be explored by a human body. [![Image 32: Eric Schaal, Dalí’s Dream of Venus pavilion at the New York World’s Fair, 1939](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Dali-2.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Dali-2.jpg) Eric Schaal, Dalí’s Dream of Venus pavilion at the New York World’s Fair, 1939 Salvador Dalí took the concept of Surrealist installation into the realm of advertising, fashion, and popular entertainment. In addition to designing windows for department stores in the 1930s, he erected the Dream of Venus pavilion at the 1939 New York World’s Fair. This full-scale fantasy environment turned Surrealist eroticism into a kind of popular burlesque. Visitors entered between two huge legs, and the interior included a grotto with a ceiling covered in inverted open umbrellas, a new version of _Rainy Taxi_, a 36-foot long sofa with a reclining nude, and seventeen women costumed as mermaids cavorting for viewers in a furnished aquarium. Surrealist exhibitions broke down conventional distinctions between art and non-art, and thwarted the consumption of creative works as commodities. In addition, the Surrealists transformed the conception of the exhibition from a neutral site for the display of objects into a creative production in its own right. The later developments of environments, happenings, and installation art are all indebted to the Surrealists’ conception of the art exhibition as an experience rather than simply a showcase for artworks. ### Bibliography [Read more about the First Papers of Surrealism exhibition at the _Tate Papers_](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/publications/tate-papers/22/duchamp-childhood-work-and-play-the-vernissage-for-first-papers-of-surrealism-new-york-1942) [Roger Schall’s photos of the 1938 Surrealist exhibition at MoMA](https://www.moma.org/artists/62329) ### Cite this page Cite this page as: Dr. Charles Cramer and Dr. Kim Grant, "Surrealist Exhibitions," in _Smarthistory_, April 8, 2020, accessed December 21, 2025, [https://smarthistory.org/surrealist-exhibitions/](https://smarthistory.org/surrealist-exhibitions/). 37.title: But Live Here? No thanks: Surrealism and Anti-fascism
37.content:
**Llenbachhaus**

**October 15, 2024 – March 2, 2025**

"The human soul is international." (Bulletin international du surréalisme [Mezinárodní Buletin Surrealismu], Prague, April 1935)

Surrealism was a political movement of international reach and internationalist conviction. While it had its origins in art and literature, it far exceeded both. Surrealists declared reality to be insufficient. Their ambition was to radically alter society and reimagine life.

As early as the dawn of the movement in the 1920s, surrealists denounced the European colonialist project. They organized against fascists, fought in the Spanish Civil War, called on Wehrmacht soldiers to commit sabotage; were detained in camps and persecuted, escaped Europe, and died in war. They wrote poems, worked on paintings and collective drawings, took photographs, assembled collages, and organized exhibitions—all of which were aimed at disarticulating a supposedly rational language in a supposedly rational world. They refused to grant the "pathetic" imaginary world of daily politics access into their art.

The government and occupation by fascist parties in Europe and throughout the world, as well as the World Wars and colonial wars, shaped Surrealism at the time of its emergence, and forced the lives of its protagonists into unpredictable trajectories. At the same time, these upheavals resulted in remarkable encounters and actions of international solidarity, whose red lines connecting links ran from Prague to Coyoacán in Mexico City, from Cairo to republican Spain, from Marseille to Fort-de-France on Martinique, from Puerto Rico and Paris to Chicago and back. Surrealist thinking and action, then as today, happened in various places simultaneously. Thus, instead of presenting a didactic, linear narrative, the exhibition is organized into several episodes, arranged like a map. The goal is to make Surrealism visible as the contentious, connected, and politicized movement its protagonists understood it to be.

Within their artistic work, the surrealists insisted on an absolute freedom that was to infect the rest of society. The surrealists' understanding stood at odds with Fascist freedom: the freedom to command and obey. For the surrealists, emancipation meant a way of life whose rhythm was not that of wage labor and whose goals were larger than the glorious Nation and bottomless Profit. They bemoaned the stunted imagination of a society for which art and poetry had become eccentric activities. "If anyone comes to tell us that our present has other things on its mind than writing poetry, we’ll reply: 'So do we!'," wrote a member of La Main à plume, a group that fought in the Resistance in occupied Paris and secretly published volumes of poetry.

Not least because of this constitutive but open relationship between art and politics, later movements repeatedly invoked Surrealism: for example, as a method that can often be linked quite naturally to emancipatory goals, it was taken up during the 1968 protests and by representatives of the Black Liberation Movement. The exhibition at Lenbachhaus is conceived as a bundling of attempts to revise a still narrowly defined and politically trivialized Surrealist canon. Our goal is to arrive, together with our public, at new answers to the question, "What is Surrealism?"

With works and texts by: Manuel Álvarez Bravo, Art & Liberté, Die Badewanne, Enrico Baj, Georges Bataille, Hans Bellmer, Erwin Blumenfeld, Victor Brauner, André Breton, Claude Cahun und Marcel Moore, Leonora Carrington, Aimé Césaire, Suzanne Césaire, Chicago Surrealists, Laura Corsiglia, Jayne Cortez, Roberto Crippa, Robert Desnos, Óscar Domínguez, Gianni Dova, Paul Éluard, Max Ernst, Erró, Esteban Francés, Eugenio Granell, Groupe Octobre, John Heartfield, Jindřich Heisler, Jacques Hérold (geb.
